questions.prompt: A small neutral molecular solute has several accessible O–H groups and only a small nonpolar region. Which interaction-based prediction is most reasonable when comparing water and hexane as solvents?
options: It must be insoluble in both because every soluble substance must form ions.
Hexane must be better because O–H groups are nonpolar and cannot interact with water.
The two solvents must dissolve identical amounts because the solute’s molar mass is unchanged.
Water is likely to be more compatible because it can form favorable hydrogen-bond contacts with the solute’s O–H groups.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Accessible O–H groups can donate and accept appropriate hydrogen-bond contacts with water, making aqueous solvation favorable relative to a nonpolar solvent for the stated small molecule. A incorrectly requires ionization for molecular dissolution. B misclassifies O–H groups and ignores their water interactions. C treats molar mass as the only factor and ignores solvent identity. This is a qualitative prediction, not a guarantee of one exact solubility or complete miscibility for every molecule containing O–H.

questions.prompt: I2 is a nonpolar molecular solute. Which explanation supports predicting greater compatibility with nonpolar hexane than with water in the usual intermolecular-interaction model?
options: Hexane converts every iodine molecule into free iodide ions without another reactant.
I2 and hexane can have favorable dispersion interactions, while introducing I2 into water does not replace water’s hydrogen-bonding environment equally well.
Water has no dispersion interactions, so it cannot attract any neutral molecule.
All nonpolar molecules have permanent positive and negative ends that form ion–dipole bonds.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Polarizable iodine molecules can interact through dispersion with a nonpolar solvent, while water’s strong solvent–solvent interactions are not compensated in the same way by this nonpolar solute. A introduces unsupported electron transfer. C falsely removes dispersion from water; all molecular species have electron-cloud fluctuations. D assigns permanent charges/dipoles to nonpolar molecules and mislabels ion–dipole interactions. The comparison is an interaction-based tendency, not a claim that iodine has exactly zero aqueous solubility.

questions.prompt: A series of neutral alcohols each has one O–H group. Their compatibility with water generally decreases as the hydrocarbon chain becomes much longer. Which explanation best accounts for the trend?
options: A larger nonpolar region must always improve water compatibility solely because the molecular mass increases.
Every alcohol must have identical solubility because each contains the same one O–H group.
The growing nonpolar region becomes a larger part of the molecule, so the same O–H group does not compensate for water interactions to the same extent.
Water becomes nonpolar whenever a long-chain alcohol is added.
questions.explanation: C is correct. A single polar group can be outweighed by a growing nonpolar region, so the balance of solute–solvent and solvent–solvent interactions changes with molecular structure. A transfers a mass/dispersion trend into an unjustified universal water-solubility rule and ignores the competing solvent interactions. B treats one functional group as sufficient to fix the behavior of the entire molecule. D changes the identity/polarity of water rather than considering the mixed interactions. The trend is qualitative and does not require a sharp universal chain-length cutoff.

questions.prompt: A student predicts that every ionic compound must be highly soluble in water because water is polar. Which response best evaluates the prediction?
options: Water can stabilize separated ions, but the prediction must also consider the interactions holding the solid together and the overall balance of interactions.
The prediction is always correct because any polar solvent completely removes every ionic attraction.
The prediction is always false because neutral water molecules cannot interact with charged ions.
The prediction is correct only if the ionic solid first becomes a set of neutral atoms.
questions.explanation: A is correct. Ion–dipole solvation can favor separation of ions, but it does not universally overcome the interactions in every ionic solid and changes in the solvent environment. B equates favorable solvation with guaranteed complete dissolution of any lattice. C ignores attraction between an ion and water’s partial charges. D requires a chemical change to neutral atoms that is not necessary for ionic dissolution. A qualitative interaction model gives a basis for comparison without claiming a universal solubility rule or requiring a Ksp calculation here.

questions.prompt: Why is hexane generally a poor solvent for NaCl compared with water?
options: Hexane has stronger permanent dipoles than water, so it repels all ions.
Water can dissolve NaCl only by changing Na+ into neutral sodium atoms.
NaCl must dissolve equally well in both solvents because its ion charges do not depend on solvent identity.
Hexane does not provide the strong conventional ion–dipole stabilization that polar water can provide to separated Na+ and Cl- ions.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Water’s dipole can stabilize separated cations and anions; nonpolar hexane does not provide comparable permanent-dipole solvation for this salt, making the strong ionic lattice difficult to offset. A incorrectly assigns strong permanent dipoles to hexane and replaces solvation with universal repulsion. B neutralizes the ions without the specified chemical electron transfer. C confuses unchanged ion identities with unchanged solute–solvent interactions; the solvent’s structure and polarity still matter. Nonpolar solvents can still have induced-dipole interactions; the point is not that every possible ion–solvent attraction is exactly zero.

questions.prompt: Two hypothetical ionic solids have similar ion sizes. One consists of +2 and −2 ions, the other of +1 and −1 ions. A student argues that stronger hydration of the doubly charged ions proves their solid is more water-soluble. Which evaluation is best?
options: The claim is guaranteed because only hydration strength matters.
The claim is guaranteed false because stronger lattice interactions alone always rule out dissolution, regardless of hydration.
The conclusion cannot follow from hydration alone, because the larger charges can also strengthen attractions within the solid.
The two solids must have identical solubility because their ion sizes are similar.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Greater charge can strengthen both ion–dipole solvation and ion–ion attractions in the original solid. Considering just the favorable side does not establish the final solubility ranking. A ignores the competing interactions. B makes the opposite one-sided argument by ignoring favorable solvation and treating lattice strength alone as decisive. D uses size alone while omitting charge and the overall balance. This question asks the limits of a qualitative argument; no lattice-energy, hydration-enthalpy, entropy, or equilibrium-constant calculation is required.

questions.prompt: A neutral molecular solute dissolves intact in a suitable molecular solvent, with no reaction. Which particle-level account is appropriate?
options: Every covalent bond inside the solute must break before any mixing can occur.
Some original solute–solute and solvent–solvent contacts are replaced by solute–solvent contacts while the molecules retain their identities.
All solute and solvent molecules must become fully separated, with no attractions remaining in the solution.
The solute must acquire a permanent full ionic charge even though the stated model is nonreactive molecular dissolution.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Mixing changes which particles interact with one another; it does not require destroying the molecules or removing every cohesive interaction. A confuses dissolution with covalent decomposition. C describes complete separation rather than a condensed molecular solution. D incorrectly requires ion formation. The relative balance of the old and new interactions helps explain compatibility, but a qualitative interaction description is not a complete quantitative thermodynamic calculation.

questions.prompt: A small polar molecule has an oxygen atom with available lone pairs but no O–H, N–H, or F–H bond. A student claims it cannot interact favorably with water because it is not a conventional hydrogen-bond donor. Which response is best?
options: Water can donate an O–H hydrogen bond to the solute’s acceptor oxygen; the solute need not also be a donor.
Any molecule without its own O–H bond can have only dispersion interactions with water.
The oxygen must form a full O2- ion before water can approach it.
Both partners must each donate and accept a hydrogen bond in every individual contact.
questions.explanation: A is correct. A solute oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from water’s O–H group, even when the solute has no conventional donor of its own. B excludes dipolar and acceptor interactions without justification. C replaces a molecular lone-pair acceptor with an unsupported full ionic species. D imposes simultaneous donor/acceptor roles on both partners in one contact; one donor and one suitable acceptor suffice. This reasoning supports favorable interactions but does not guarantee that every such molecule is fully miscible with water.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the usefulness of the phrase “like dissolves like”?
options: It guarantees complete miscibility between every pair of polar substances.
It proves every nonpolar molecule has exactly zero solubility in water.
It is a qualitative guide based on compatible intermolecular interactions, with the full molecular structures and competing interactions still relevant.
It means substances dissolve only when solute and solvent have the same molecular formula.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Similar interaction types often make mixing favorable, but the phrase is a tendency rather than an exact universal law. A makes polarity alone a guarantee despite differences in structure and interaction balance. B replaces low compatibility with an absolute zero-solubility claim. D confuses similar interactions with identical chemical identity. A useful model should explain trends while acknowledging what it cannot quantify or guarantee from a single label.

questions.prompt: Two liquids form separate bulk layers, but reliable analysis detects a small dissolved amount of each liquid in the other layer. Which interpretation is consistent with solubility concepts?
options: Two layers prove every detected cross-layer molecule must have changed its molecular formula.
Limited mutual solubility can coexist with bulk phase separation; separate layers do not require exactly zero molecules of the other component.
The two layers must have equal composition because the liquids were shaken together.
Any detected molecule in the other layer proves complete miscibility, regardless of the persistent separate phases.
questions.explanation: B is correct. A system can have finite but limited mutual solubility and still separate into phases with different compositions. A invokes chemical change rather than physical partitioning. C assumes shaking guarantees equal equilibrium composition. D confuses a small dissolved amount with unlimited mixing into one homogeneous phase. The analysis is stipulated reliable, so the question does not ask students to diagnose sampling contamination or calculate a distribution coefficient.

questions.prompt: Adding some ethanol to water increases the dissolved amount of a particular nonpolar molecular solute in a given experiment. Ethanol contains both an O–H group and a small hydrocarbon region. Which structural explanation is consistent with this observation?
options: Ethanol must convert the nonpolar solute into a new ionic compound before it can dissolve.
Once ethanol is present, only water–water contacts matter; solute–solvent contacts remain irrelevant.
Any increase in solubility requires exactly equal numbers of water and solute molecules.
Ethanol can maintain favorable contacts with water through its O–H group while offering additional nonpolar-region interactions with the solute.
questions.explanation: D is correct. A solvent component with both polar and nonpolar regions can change the balance of interactions and help accommodate the stated solute in the solvent mixture. A requires an unsupported chemical ionization. B excludes the new solute–solvent contacts that can change the balance of interactions. C imposes a fixed one-to-one mixture ratio not required by the observation or by solution behavior. The observation is supplied; the explanation does not claim that ethanol makes every nonpolar compound infinitely soluble or that all solvent mixtures behave identically.
